en: The Therī-Apadāna Ekūposathika Vagga 7.
The Apadāna of the Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī
Once, the Lamp of the World,
in the Great Forest at Vesālī,
was in the gabled hall of the excellent assembly hall.
The Charioteer of Men was dwelling there.
At that time, the Jina’s maternal aunt,
the bhikkhunī Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, [was also there].
There, in that delightful city,
he dwelt in a nunnery belonging to liberated bhikkhunīs.
Together with five hundred [monks];
thus, when she had gone into seclusion,
this was the thought that arose in her mind.
“The Parinibbāna of the Buddha,
or that of the Pair of Chief Disciples,
or the joy of Rāhula and Ānanda— ”
I shall not be able to see either the Parinibbāna of the Buddha or that of the Pair of Chief Disciples.
Of Mahākassapa and Nanda,
and of Ānanda and Rāhula, they [all] prematurely abandoned the life-formations.
Having established myself in Nibbāna,
may I go forth, authorized by the Great Seer, the Lord of the World.”
Likewise, there was the reflection of five hundred bhikkhunīs,
including Khemā and the others.
This very thing was reflected upon.
At that time there was an earthquake,
and the drums of the gods resounded.
The deities dwelling in their retreats, oppressed by grief,
lamented most piteously.
There the tears flowed forth; the bhikkhunīs,
having approached Gotamī, [spoke].
Bowing their heads at his feet,
they spoke these words:
"Having been sprinkled there with drops of water,"
While Mayā and Mayī were in private,
the earth trembled and shook,
and the drums of the gods resounded.
Lamentations were heard;
for what purpose indeed did Gotamī speak all that at that time? She then spoke it all.
Just as they had each reflected,
so too did they all speak exactly as they had reflected.
“If it pleases you, noble lady,
that Nibbāna is the supreme bliss;
then we all shall attain Nibbāna.”
O venerable ones, with the Buddha’s permission,
we have indeed gone forth from both the household life and from existence itself.
Together indeed we shall go to Nibbāna, the supreme state.
As we are going toward Nibbāna,
"What shall I say? she said,
and then she departed together with all of them from the nunnery.
“May those deities who dwell in this monastery forgive me;
this [is for] the dwelling place of the bhikkhunīs.”
This is my last sight of the world,
where there is neither old age nor death,
nor meeting with those who are unpleasant.
"There shall be no separation from what is dear;
I shall go to that unconditioned state.
Hearing this, those who were not yet free from passion—
Hearing the words of the Sugata’s son,
they lamented in their grief,
"Alas! How little merit we have!"
The nunnery is empty;
it has become devoid of them,
like the stars at dawn.
The sons of the Conqueror are not seen.
Gotamī attains nibbāna together with five hundred [disciples].
Just as the Ganges flows to the ocean together with a hundred tributary rivers,
so do they proceed along the royal highway.
Having seen him, the faithful female lay follower went out from her home, prostrated at his feet,
and spoke these words.
“Be gracious, O possessor of great wealth!
Having abandoned us who are without a protector,
it is not fitting for you to enter final nirvana.”
They lamented there out of longing.
To dispel their sorrow,
he spoke these sweet words:
“Enough of weeping, my sons;
this is now the time for you to laugh.
Suffering has been fully understood by me.”
The cause of suffering has been avoided;
cessation has been realized by me,
and the path has also been well-cultivated.
The first recitation section.
The Teacher has been served by me;
the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
The heavy burden has been laid down;
the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
That for whose sake we went forth—
From the home to the homeless life;
that goal has been attained by me:
the destruction of all fetters.
As long as the Buddha and his True Dharma remain undiminished,
so long shall it be time for me to pass into Nibbāna.
"Do not grieve for me, little girls.
Koṇḍañña, Ānanda, Nanda,
and others remain, as do Rāhula and the Victor."
The Saṅgha is happy and united,
while the heretics have been struck down;
the glory of the Okkāka lineage—
The crusher of Māra has risen;
O little daughter, is this not the very time for me to seek Nibbāna?
That which I have long desired is fulfilled today;
this is the time for the sounding of the drums of joy.
Why these tears, little sons?
If you have affection for me,
and if there is gratitude in you;
For the sake of the endurance of the true Dhamma,
all of you exert firm energy.
Thina gave him the going forth.
The Perfectly Awakened One was entreated by me;
therefore, follow him in such a way that I shall rejoice.
Having thus instructed them and being escorted by the bhikkhunīs,
she approached the Buddha and paid him homage.
He spoke these words:
"O Sugata, I am your mother;
and you, O Hero, are my father."
O Lord, giver of the true Dhamma,
by you I was born, O Gotama;
and I have been nurtured by you, O Sugata.
The physical body was mine for you;
the irreproachable Dhamma-body has been nurtured by me through you.
For a moment you were a subduer of craving;
you were made to drink milk by me,
and by you I have been led to ultimate peace.
For you have been fed the milk of the Dhamma.
O Great Sage, you owe me nothing for my protection from bondage.
Women who desire sons obtain such a son as they pray for,
even like those of the great kings beginning with Mandhātā.
She who was my mother, submerged in the ocean of existence,
has been carried across the sea of becoming by you, my son.
"Queen, mother of the king"—
this is a name easily obtained by women;
but that which is called "Mother of the Buddha," [is rare].
This is most difficult to obtain.
And yet, O Great Hero,
you have fulfilled that aspiration of mine.
Whether small or great,
all that has been filled by me.
I wish to attain final Nibbāna.
Having cast off this body,
grant me your permission, O Hero,
Leader who brings an end to suffering.
Stretch out your feet, which are as soft as lotuses and adorned with wheels, goads, banners,
and calluses; homage be to you!
I shall bring forth a most excellent son.
Make your body visible, resembling a heap of gold.
"Having well beheld your body,
O Leader, I go to peace—
[the body] endowed with the thirty-two marks."
The Conqueror showed his mother his body, adorned with excellent marks, as radiant as the young sun at the break of dawn.
With the soles of his feet marked with wheels, resembling full-blown lotuses and possessing the splendor of the rising sun;
Then she prostrated with her head:
“I bow to you, O Sun among Men,
the banner of the Solar dynasty.”
At my final death,
O Foremost One in the World, I shall not see those women again.
Are considered the source of all faults;
if there is any fault in me, may you,
O Maker of Compassion, forgive it.
And for the going forth of women,
I entreated you again and again;
if there is any fault in me regarding that, [please forgive me].
Forgive that, O bull among men.
O Hero, it was with your permission that the bhikkhunīs were instructed by me.
“If there is anything ill-spoken therein,
forgive it, O Lord of Forgiveness.
“One must indeed forgive that which is not forgiven;”
What more shall I say to you, who are adorned with virtues and who are departing for Nibbāna?
When my Saṅgha of bhikkhus is pure and complete,
and the worlds are able to escape from here,
[I shall teach] those who have fallen into calamity at the break of dawn.
Having seen this, the other bhikkhunīs followed the Supreme Victor,
just as the moon follows Tārā to Mount Sumeru.
Having circumambulated him and bowed at his feet,
she stood gazing into his face:
"I have never before been satiated by the sight of you."
The eye is not the ear according to your teaching;
my mind alone, having attained that [teaching],
is satisfied by the flavor of the Dhamma.
O you who strike the instruments to be played amidst the assembly,
those who shall behold your face—
Blessed are you, O bull among men!
Your fingers are long, your nails are copper-colored,
and your heels are beautiful and broad.
Those who shall bow at his feet,
O bearer of virtues, they too are fortunate;
for his smiles are sweet.
And those words which are heard— both fault-finding and beneficial—
are also fortunate, O Supreme among Men.
Fortunate am I, O Great Hero,
intent upon worshipping your feet;
I have crossed the wilderness of saṃsāra.
With well-spoken words, she [addressed] the fortunate one.
Then, having made the proclamation,
that woman of excellent vows also addressed the community of monks.
Having paid homage to Rāhula and Ānanda, he spoke these words:
“O you who resemble the lairs of venomous serpents!”
In this body, an abode of disease,
one should become disenchanted with this mass of suffering,
which has aging and death as its domain.
In this world strewn with various stains of defilement, dependent on others, and devoid of agency,
I desire to attain extinction through that [means].
“Grant your permission, my sons.
Nanda and the auspicious Rāhula,
free from sorrow and free from taints, [responded].
Firmly established in immovable stability,
he reflected upon the nature of phenomena:
"Shame on the conditioned, which is fickle!"
It is pithless like a plantain tree,
resembling an illusion or a mirage—
fleeting and unstable.
That even this Gotamī, the maternal aunt of the Victor and the nurse of the Buddha,
should meet her end— how strange!
"All that is conditioned is impermanent.
At that time, Ānanda was still a trainee,
overcome with grief for the Beloved of the Victor.
Making his tears flow there, he lamented piteously: "Alas!
Gotamī goes toward peace."
Surely even the Buddha will go to extinction before long,
like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.
To Ānanda, who was thus lamenting, Gotamī said:
"O you who are as deep as the ocean of your learning— "
Devoted to attending upon the Buddha:
“It is not right to grieve, my son,
now that he has appeared at a time for joy.”
"By you, my son, refuge has been found for me;
that Nibbāna has been reached by you.
By you, dear one, it was requested,"
He granted us the going forth;
do not be despondent, my son,
for your exertion has borne fruit.
That state which was not seen by those of old,
nor even by the teachers of other sects—
that state [is attained] by delicate women.
It has been known for seven years.
O protector of the Buddha’s teaching,
this is your final sight of me.
"Therefore, my son, I shall go where,
having gone, one is no longer seen;
perhaps while teaching the Dhamma,"
The Leader of the World threw [the flower];
then, out of compassion, I spoke these words of aspiration.
“Live long, O Great Hero;
remain for an eon, O Great Sage,
for the benefit of the entire world.”
“May you be free from old age and death.
To me, who spoke thus, the Buddha said this:
“Buddhas are not to be venerated in the manner that you venerate them, Gotamī. “How then,
O All-Knowing One, [should they be venerated]?”
The Tathāgatas are to be venerated;
how it is that the Buddhas are not to be venerated—
explain that to me when I ask you.
“Behold the disciples who are harmonious, ardent in energy, resolute, and always firm in their exertion.”
"This was my salutation to the Buddhas.
Then, having gone to my dwelling,
I reflected all alone:
“The Lord, who has reached the end of the three worlds, has restrained this assembly;
well then, I shall attain final Nibbāna.”
"May I not see misfortune";
having thought thus,
I beheld the Seventh Sage.
I informed the Leader of the time of my parinibbāna;
then he gave his consent.
“Know the time, Gotamī.
The defilements have been incinerated by me;
…pe…
I dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed has come to me... [as before] ...
Such is the teaching of the Buddha.
The four analytical knowledges... [and so forth]...
“The teaching of the Buddha has been proclaimed.
Those fools who have fallen into doubt regarding the realization of the Dhamma— ”
“O Gotamī, show your supernormal power for the sake of abandoning their wrong views. Then,
having prostrated to the Fully Awakened One, she—
Leaping up into the sky,
Gotamī, by the Buddha’s permission, displayed manifold supernormal powers.
Being one, she became many;
being many, she likewise became one;
she appeared and vanished.
Through walls and through mountains she went;
unimpeded, she moved,
even sinking into the ground.
He walked upon the water as if on dry land,
and likewise through the air like a bird.
Then, moving in the cross-legged posture,
he exercised mastery with his body as far as the abode of Brahmā.
Having made Mount Sineru a staff and the great earth an umbrella,
he overturned it along with its roots.
Walking in the sky while maintaining his concentration,
he made the world misty, as if at the time of six suns rising.
Like the world at the end of an eon,
she made it filled with garlands of flames;
[she approached] the great rock of Mucalinda.
Within the space at the foot of Mount Meru,
he grasped all the mustard seeds with a single fist.
He covered it with the tip of his finger,
including the sun and the moon;
thousands of moons and suns—
He held [the waters] like a garland;
he bore the waters of the four oceans with a single hand.
Having the appearance of clouds at the end of an eon,
rain down a great shower upon the Wheel-turning Monarch and his retinue.
She measured out the surface of the sky;
she displayed a garuḍa, an elephant, and a lion,
all roaring aloud.
Having manifested herself alone as an immeasurable multitude of bhikkhunīs,
she then made them disappear once more.
Ekikā spoke to the Sage:
“O Great Hero, your maternal aunt is one who carries out your teaching.”
“Having attained my own goal,
I bow at your feet, O Visionary One.
Having displayed various supernormal powers, he said:
Having descended from the sky and paid homage to the Lamp of the World,
she sat down to one side.
“I am one hundred and twenty years of age,
O Great Sage;
enough of this, O Hero.”
“I shall attain Nibbāna, O Leader!
Then the entire assembly, utterly amazed, stood with palms joined in reverence.
“Noble lady, how was it for you,
who possessed incomparable psychic power and exertion?
“There was a Victor named Padumuttara.”
The Visionary among all phenomena;
a hundred thousand aeons from now, a Leader appeared.
At that time, I was born in Haṃsavatī into a family of death-wardens,
who were fully endowed with every kind of assistance.
Prosperous, flourishing, and possessing great wealth,
she was once attended by a multitude of female slaves while in the company of her father.
With a great retinue,
he approached that Bull among Men,
who was raining down like Vāsava.
The cloud of Dhamma, free from taints,
resembling the autumnal sun,
blazing with a network of rays.
Having seen her and gladdened his heart,
and having heard her well-spoken words,
[he placed] the Bhikkhunī, his mother’s sister, in the foremost position.
Having heard that the Leader of Men was about to depart,
they gave a great gift to that Tathāgata for seven days.
Having prostrated at the feet of the Bull among Men and his Saṅgha,
[he offered] many requisites.
I aspired for that state;
then the Seventh Sage spoke to the great assembly.
“I shall proclaim the merit of her who fed the Leader of the World together with the Saṅgha for seven days.”
Listen as I speak:
in a hundred thousand aeons hence,
one born of the Okkāka clan shall appear.
One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world;
he will have heirs in his teachings.
Born from her own breast and fashioned by the Dhamma,
she shall be a female disciple of the Teacher, known by the name Gotamī.
She is the maternal aunt of that Buddha,
the one who restored his life;
she holds the preeminence among those of long-standing seniority.
‘The monks will receive [offerings] from the bhikkhunīs. Having heard that and rejoiced,
he then served the Jina for as long as he lived.
Having appeared through conditions,
I then passed away among the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
In the fulfillment of all desires,
having been reborn with ten qualities,
I surpassed others.
By means of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
and by means of vitality and beauty, too.
And with happiness and fame as well.
Likewise, having attained sovereignty, may I shine forth.
There I was the beloved chief queen of the Lord of the Immortals.
Wandering thus through this cycle of existence, I—
Impelled by the wind of karma,
I was born in the village of Dāsaka within the realm of King Kāsī.
At that time, one hundred and five less than fifteen hundred [beings] dwell there;
of them all, he who is the eldest—
I became his wife.
Five hundred Self-Enlightened Ones entered the village for alms.
Seeing them, I was delighted along with all the women;
having become a group, we all—
We attended upon him for four months;
having given him the three robes,
we wandered through saṃsāra together with our husbands.
Having passed away from there,
we have all gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
and now, in our final existence, we—
I was born in the city of Devadaha.
My father was Añjana-Sakka,
and my mother was Sulakkhaṇā.
Then she went to the house of Suddhodana in Kapilavatthu;
the others were born into the Sakya clan.
They came to the home of the Sakyans;
I was the most distinguished among them all,
for I was the one who helped the Victor to his seat.
My son went forth from home and became a Buddha, a leader;
afterwards, I too went forth.
Together with five hundred wise Śākyan women,
I attained the bliss of peace.
Those who were our masters in a previous birth,
performing meritorious deeds together with us—
They were makers of the great covenant;
having been shown compassion by the Sugata,
they touched the state of arhatship.
The other bhikkhunīs ascended into the vault of the sky,
like a cluster of stars gathered together.
Possessing great psychic power, they shone brightly;
they displayed manifold miracles,
like a variety of ornaments.
Like a well-trained smith with gold that is workable,
having displayed his miraculous feats, he—
Having then delighted the eminent speaker, the Sage, together with his assembly, with many diverse verses.
Having descended from the sky and paid homage to the Best of Sages,
she was granted permission by the Leader of Men.
They sat down each in their proper place.
“We have been very compassionate toward us all for a long time, O Gotamī.”
O Vāsitā, through your merits,
we have attained the destruction of the taints;
our defilements have been incinerated.
All states of existence have been utterly eradicated;
like a serpent that has severed its bonds,
we dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed has come to us in the presence of the Best of Buddhas;
the three knowledges have been attained.
Such is the teaching of the Buddha:
the four analytical knowledges and these eight liberations.
The six direct knowledges have been realized;
the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
We have mastery over the supernormal powers.
With the divine ear-element and the knowledge of penetrating the minds of others,
we have attained mastery, O Great Sage.
We know our former births,
our divine eye is purified,
and all taints are utterly destroyed.
Now there is no further becoming. There exists [mastery] in the meaning, in the Dhamma, in the phrasing,
and in the inspired eloquence.
Knowledge has arisen within us, O Great Hero, in your presence.
You have been served by us.
For they possess hearts of loving-kindness, O Leader;
grant permission for all of them,
O Great Sage, for the sake of Nibbāna.
“‘We shall attain Nibbāna’—this is what you say;
what more shall I say to you now? For the time has come for you.”
"Do you think so? the Conqueror said.
Then those bhikkhunīs, headed by Gotamī, [spoke] to the Conqueror.
Having paid homage,
they rose from their seats and departed with a great multitude of people.
Accompanied by the Leader of the World,
that Hero wandered as far as his mother’s well.
Then Gotamī fell at the feet of the Kinsman of the World,
together with all of them.
“This is the final salutation at his feet.
This is my last sight of the Lord of the World.”
Never again shall I behold your face, which has the form of the Deathless; nor,
O Hero, shall there be for me another salutation.
It shall touch your most tender feet,
O Foremost One in the World;
today I go to final peace.
“What is the use of this form to you,
as it truly is in this very life?
All this is merely conditioned.”
"which offers no consolation and is but temporary.
Having gone with them to her own nunnery, she—
Folding his legs in the half-lotus posture,
he sat upon the supreme seat. Then,
at that place, the female lay devotee—
Devoted to the Buddha’s teaching;
having heard of her conduct,
they approached to pay homage at her feet.
Strike your chest and rend it,
like a creeper whose roots have been severed,
wailing with piteous cries!
Overcome by grief, they fell to the ground:
“O Lord who grants refuge,
do not go away to final nirvana, abandoning us!”
Having prostrated ourselves, we all entreat you with our heads bowed:
"She who is the foremost among those striving..."
Faith and wisdom are the laywoman’s head;
while massaging her head,
he spoke these words.
“Enough, my son, with despondency,
which follows the snares of Māra;
all that is conditioned is impermanent.”
“Ending in separation, unstable and fleeting.
Then, having dismissed them,
she attained the supreme first jhāna.
He attained the second, the third, and the fourth [jhānas],
as well as the base of infinite space.
Likewise the sphere of consciousness,
nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
he entered these in due order.
Gautamī entered the jhānas in reverse order,
down as far as the first jhāna.
Then he reached the fourth [jhāna].
Emerging from that, he attained Nibbāna,
like a lamp going out, free from all taints.
There was a great earthquake,
lightning flashed from the sky,
and drums resounded.
The deities lamented,
and a rain of flowers fell from the sky upon the earth.
Even Meru, the king of mountains,
trembled like an actor on the stage,
appearing exceedingly pale with grief.
The ocean became tumultuous;
at that moment, the gods, nāgas, asuras, and Brahmā were filled with awe.
“Impermanent indeed are conditioned things,
for they have come to this dissolution.
Those who once surrounded me...”
She was one who carried out the Teacher’s instruction;
through non-clinging,
she too was extinguished like a lamp.
Alas, unions end in separation!
Alas, all that is conditioned is impermanent!
Alas, life ends in destruction!
Such was the lamentation.
Then the gods and Brahmā [performed] the following of worldly custom;
Having approached the Seventh Sage, they acted in accordance with the time.
Then the Teacher addressed them:
To Ānanda, the ocean of sons, [he said]: “Go, Ānanda,
announce the passing away of the Bhikkhus’ mother.”
Then Ānanda, joyless and with eyes full of tears,
spoke in a faltering voice:
“Let the bhikkhus assemble,
from the east, the south, the west,
and from the vicinity of the north.”
Listen to my speech,
O bhikkhus who are the children of the Sugata;
that which she increased with diligent effort—
This was the final body of the Sage;
Gotamī has gone to peace,
like a star at the rising of the sun.
Having established the designation "Mother of the Buddha," which is peerless,
there is no place where even the Five-Eyed One has gone.
The Leader will behold their destination:
those who have faith in the Sugata and who are dear to the Great Sage.
"Let the one who is the essence of the Sugata pay honor to the Mother of the Buddha.
Hearing this, even from afar, [they]...
"Come quickly, O monks!
Some by the power of the Buddha,
and some skilled in supernormal powers."
In a delightful, excellent gabled chamber,
beautiful and made entirely of gold,
they placed a couch.
Wherever you lay down, Gotamī,
the four world-protectors supported you upon their shoulders.
The remaining deities, led by Sakka,
gathered together in the gabled halls;
all the gabled halls—
There were even five hundred [palaces],
possessing the colors of autumn and the sun,
for they were fashioned by Vissakamma.
All those bhikkhunīs had been lying on couches,
having ascended the shoulders of the gods.
They departed one after another.
The surface of the sky was completely covered by a canopy.
The moon and sun, marked with the seven stars and made of gold,
and many banners were raised aloft.
A cloak of flowers was spread out;
sky-lotuses descended, and a flower rose up from the earth.
The moon and sun are visible,
and the stars blaze forth;
even when the sun has reached the meridian, it is seen.
He did not cause distress as the moon does.
The gods [honored him] with divine scents and fragrant garlands.
With instrumental music, dances,
and choral performances, they made offerings;
so too did the nāgas, asuras, and brahmas.
According to their means and according to their strength,
they honored the Mother of the Buddha as she was being carried forth, now extinguished.
All have been led forward and attained extinction through the milk of the Sugata;
Gotamī alone is being led away behind.
Honored as the nourishers of the Buddhas,
they stand before the gods and humans,
together with the nāgas, asuras, and brahmās.
Later, the Buddha, accompanied by his disciple,
went to honor his mother.
[Then occurred] the Parinibbāna of the Buddha.
It was not as it has been before;
the final passing away of Gotamī was indeed extraordinary.
O monks, the Buddha does not envy the Nibbāna of another Buddha;
the Buddha [rejoices] in the Nibbāna of Gotamī.
Sāriputta and the others did likewise;
having constructed funeral pyres made entirely of fragrant substances, they—
They burned those [bodies] there, strewn with fragrant powders;
the remaining portions were consumed by the flames.
Only bones remained entirely;
and then Ānanda spoke these words that inspire a sense of spiritual urgency.
“Gotamī has passed away;
her little body is being cremated.
The meeting with the Buddha’s Nibbāna—”
"It will not be long before it happens.
Then he took the relics of Gotamī that were contained within her bowl.
Urged by the Buddha, Ānanda offered them to the Lord;
taking them up with his hand, he...
The Best of Sages said:
"Just as when a great,
sturdy tree stands firm..."
Just as that greater trunk might decay through impermanence,
so too [it may happen] for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs.
Gotamī has attained final Nibbāna.
Oh, what a marvel for me,
that even my mother has passed into Nibbāna!
When nothing remains but the physical body, there is no sorrow or lamentation.
That which belongs to others is not to be grieved for.
They have crossed the ocean of saṃsāra;
having avoided all torment,
they have become cool and attained perfect peace.
You are wise and possessed of great insight,
as well as broad insight;
you are one who has long been known among the bhikkhunīs.
Thus, O bhikkhus, you should remember:
he was master of the supernormal powers and possessed the divine ear-element.
Gotamī attained mastery over the knowledge of the minds of others,
and she knew her former births.
The divine eye has been purified;
all taints are utterly exhausted,
and for her there is no further becoming.
Regarding the meanings, the phenomena, the definitions,
and likewise regarding inspired eloquence,
his knowledge was completely purified.
Therefore, she is not to be grieved for,
any more than a blazing fire struck by an iron hammer.
Just as the destination of one who has gradually attained peace is not known,
so it is for those who are rightly liberated.
For those who have crossed over the flood of the bonds of sensual desire and attained unshakable happiness, there is no way to describe their destination.
Therefore, be islands unto yourselves,
with mindfulness as your domain;
having cultivated the seven factors of enlightenment, [be lamps unto yourselves].
"You shall make an end of suffering.
Thus indeed did the Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī speak these verses.
This is the seventh legend of the Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
